_help: Exam-style practice questions (written for this site — not official Pearson questions). A story appears under a question when it has one of the question's tags; it appears under a strand when its text also matches one of the strand's 'match' keywords (same syntax as spec.json). Strand 'tags' (optional) narrows which stories count for that strand. Hints give recent examples — check dates before using them.

evaluate.label: 30-mark essay
evaluate.tip: Argue both for and against the view, weigh the arguments and reach a substantiated judgement. Paper 2 essays must also draw on Component 1 (synoptic).

ideas.label: 24-mark ideas essay
ideas.tip: Named thinkers from the spec carry the marks. Use news only to illustrate a point, and cover both sides.

examine.label: 12-mark 'Examine'
examine.tip: Compare the two sides point by point (similarities and differences). No overall judgement needed.

analyse.label: 12-mark 'Analyse'
analyse.tip: Explain the differences and why they exist. 3A: use at least one comparative theory (rational, cultural, structural). 3B: link to core political ideas.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the UK is experiencing a participation crisis.

sides.b: No: participation is changing, not collapsing

strands.title: Turnout is low and falling
strands.hint: 2024 general election turnout was 59.7%, the lowest since 2001. Turnout at the May 2026 Scottish Parliament election fell to about 53%.

strands.title: Trust and party membership are weak
strands.hint: Labour's membership fell by about a fifth during 2025 (figures published Aug 2026).

strands.title: New forms of participation are thriving
strands.hint: E-petitions, protests and campaigns show engagement outside elections, e.g. the 'Unite the Kingdom' rally in London on 13 Sept 2025 (estimates of 110,000–150,000 people).

strands.title: Some contests show rising engagement
strands.hint: Turnout at the May 2026 Senedd election (51.6%) was the highest ever for a Welsh devolved election. Green Party membership passed 200,000 in March 2026.

questions.judgement: Distinguish declining traditional participation (voting, party membership) from growing alternative participation. The 'crisis' is patchy, not total.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the voting age should be lowered to 16 for all UK elections.

strands.title: Consistency with Scotland and Wales
strands.hint: 16- and 17-year-olds already vote in Scottish Parliament and Senedd elections, including the May 2026 Senedd election.

strands.title: Part of a wider push to boost participation
strands.hint: The Representation of the People Bill (introduced Feb 2026; in the Lords from Sept 2026) would lower the voting age to 16 and create powers to extend automatic voter registration.

strands.title: Maturity and low youth turnout
strands.hint: Critics argue 16-year-olds lack experience and point to low youth turnout.

strands.title: Accusations of partisan motives
strands.hint: Opponents claim franchise changes are designed to help the governing party.

questions.judgement: Weigh principle (consistency, rights) against practice (turnout, maturity). The devolved experience is your best evidence.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that pressure groups have a positive impact on UK democracy.

strands.title: They win concessions and represent people between elections
strands.hint: After farmers' protests, the government raised the inheritance-tax relief threshold for farms from £1m to £2.5m (Dec 2025).

strands.title: Expertise and scrutiny
strands.hint: Think tanks and charities such as the IFS, Resolution Foundation and Institute for Government supply evidence to MPs and the media.

strands.title: Unequal influence and elitism
strands.hint: Wealthy donors and insider groups get access others don't, and lobbying rows keep recurring.

strands.title: Direct action can undermine democracy
strands.hint: Palestine Action was proscribed in July 2025, and thousands have been arrested for showing support. The Supreme Court gave permission to appeal in July 2026.

questions.judgement: Pluralist vs elitist views: groups enhance democracy when access is open and methods are lawful.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that rights are well protected in the UK.

strands.title: Courts and the Human Rights Act
strands.hint: Judicial review lets courts check ministers. The High Court ruled the Palestine Action ban unlawful in Feb 2026, although the Court of Appeal reversed this in June 2026.

strands.title: Parliament, pressure groups and the EHRC
strands.hint: Liberty, Amnesty and Parliament's Joint Committee on Human Rights challenge rights-restricting laws.

strands.title: Parliamentary sovereignty lets governments restrict rights
strands.hint: Critics point to new public-order laws (e.g. the Crime and Policing Act 2026) and the Immigration and Asylum Bill (2026), which narrows how Article 8 applies.

strands.title: Pressure to leave the ECHR
strands.hint: The Conservatives (Oct 2025) and Reform UK both pledge to leave the ECHR.

questions.judgement: Rights rest mainly on ordinary statute and convention, so how secure they are depends on political will.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the UK now has a multi-party system.

strands.title: Votes are spread across five parties
strands.hint: The BBC's projected national share at the May 2026 local elections was Reform 26%, Green 18%, Labour 17%, Conservative 17%, Lib Dem 16%.

strands.title: Minor parties win seats and power
strands.hint: Plaid Cymru governs Wales (from May 2026). Reform gained about 1,450 councillors in May 2026. The Greens won the Gorton & Denton by-election (Feb 2026).

strands.title: FPTP still delivers two-party dominance at Westminster
strands.hint: In 2024 Labour won 411 seats on 33.7% of the vote, while Reform won 5 seats on 14.3%.

strands.title: Labour and the Conservatives still form government and opposition
strands.hint: Burnham leads a Labour majority government; the Conservatives are still the official opposition.

questions.judgement: Separate the party system in votes (multi-party) from seats and government at Westminster (two-party dominant).

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the Labour Party has abandoned its traditional socialist values.

strands.title: Fiscal caution and welfare restraint
strands.hint: In July 2025, 49 Labour MPs voted against the government's welfare bill even after the PIP cuts were dropped.

strands.title: Tough line on immigration
strands.hint: The Immigration and Asylum Bill passed second reading 264–90 (July 2026), with 14 Labour MPs voting against.

strands.title: Public ownership and workers' rights
strands.hint: Employment Rights Act 2025. Steel nationalisation was in the May 2026 King's Speech.

strands.title: Redistribution to cut poverty
strands.hint: The two-child benefit limit was scrapped from April 2026 (Budget, Nov 2025).

questions.judgement: Labour has always balanced socialist values with electability. Compare the current party with New Labour's Third Way.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the Conservative Party has abandoned one-nation conservatism.

strands.title: Shift right on the ECHR and immigration
strands.hint: Kemi Badenoch pledged to leave the ECHR in Oct 2025.

strands.title: Competing with Reform UK
strands.hint: Robert Jenrick defected to Reform the day he was sacked from the shadow cabinet (Jan 2026).

strands.title: One-nation voices remain
strands.hint: Badenoch's Aug 2026 reshuffle made Tom Tugendhat Shadow Foreign Secretary.

strands.title: Pragmatic offers on public services
strands.hint: Look for Conservative policies on the NHS, cost of living and public services.

questions.judgement: Use the one-nation vs New Right tension from your conservatism notes.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that minor parties have little influence in UK politics.

strands.title: FPTP blocks them at Westminster
strands.hint: Reform won 14.3% of the vote but only 5 seats in 2024.

strands.title: They win elections and run governments
strands.hint: Plaid governs Wales, the SNP governs Scotland, and Reform runs councils after May 2026.

strands.title: They push the big parties' agendas
strands.hint: Immigration policy hardened across the main parties as Reform rose in the polls.

strands.title: They crowd the polls
strands.hint: Polls in Sept 2026 had Reform within a few points of Labour (Opinium, 9–11 Sept: Labour 27%, Reform 25%, Conservatives 19%, Greens 11%, Lib Dems 10%).

questions.judgement: Influence is not the same as seats: weigh agenda-setting, devolved power and pressure on the big two.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that party funding in the UK should be reformed.

strands.title: Big donors can buy influence
strands.hint: Christopher Harborne gave Reform UK £9m in Q3 2025, reported as the largest donation on record from a living person.

strands.title: Risk of foreign interference
strands.hint: The Rycroft Review (Mar 2026) recommended pausing crypto donations. The Representation of the People Bill caps donations from overseas electors.

strands.title: State funding is unpopular and costly
strands.hint: Taxpayer funding of parties has little public support.

strands.title: Transparency rules already exist
strands.hint: Donations over the reporting threshold are published by the Electoral Commission.

questions.judgement: Weigh fairness and trust against free expression and the cost and unpopularity of state funding.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that first-past-the-post should be replaced for general elections.

strands.title: Disproportional outcomes
strands.hint: In 2024 Labour won 63% of seats on 33.7% of the vote; the Greens won 4 seats on 6.4%.

strands.title: PR works elsewhere in the UK
strands.hint: The first closed-list Senedd election (May 2026) produced a Plaid minority government. Holyrood uses AMS.

strands.title: Strong single-party government
strands.hint: FPTP usually produces majorities that can deliver a manifesto, and voters can hold them to account.

strands.title: Constituency link and public support
strands.hint: Voters rejected the Alternative Vote in the 2011 referendum.

questions.judgement: Compare how the systems perform using the devolved elections; whether reform happens depends on who benefits.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that referendums should be used more often in the UK.

strands.title: Legitimacy for big constitutional questions
strands.hint: Calls for independence referendums and border polls show demand for direct say on the constitution.

strands.title: Divisive and oversimplified
strands.hint: Brexit's legacy is often cited as a warning.

strands.title: Undermines representative democracy
strands.hint: Referendums can bypass the deliberation of Parliament.

questions.judgement: Referendums settle issues only when turnout and margins are decisive.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that social class is no longer the main factor explaining voting behaviour in the UK.

sides.a: Class is no longer the main factor

strands.title: Age and education now divide voters more
strands.hint: Age and education gaps have grown as class dealignment has continued.

strands.title: Leaders and competence (valence)
strands.hint: After becoming PM, Andy Burnham was the only party leader with a positive net rating (Opinium, Sept 2026).

strands.title: Class still shapes votes, in new ways
strands.hint: Reform's support is strongest among working-class voters.

questions.judgement: Class dealignment is real, but class interacts with age and education. Use your three election case studies.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the media has a significant influence on political outcomes in the UK.

strands.title: Investigations drive the political agenda
strands.hint: A Channel 4 News undercover investigation (Sept 2026) was followed by a Met Police inquiry into Reform's donations.

strands.title: Social media shapes campaigns
strands.hint: The Electoral Commission's report on the 2026 Senedd election (Sept 2026) raised concerns about misinformation and abuse of candidates.

strands.title: Regulation and impartiality limit broadcasters
strands.hint: Ofcom enforces due impartiality on TV and radio.

strands.title: Voters filter what they see
strands.hint: Reinforcement theory: people seek out media that confirms what they already think.

questions.judgement: The media shapes which issues matter (agenda-setting) more than it changes individual votes directly.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the UK constitution should be codified.

strands.title: Conventions are fragile
strands.hint: The first assisted dying bill fell when the session ended in April 2026 because peers tabled so many amendments that it could not finish its Lords stages. Public lawyer Mark Elliott asked whether this was 'a constitutional outrage' (he argued it was not). The episode shows how much rests on unwritten conventions.

strands.title: Rights and devolution aren't entrenched
strands.hint: Both the Human Rights Act and the devolution settlements can be changed by a simple Act of Parliament.

strands.title: Flexibility lets it evolve
strands.hint: The House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026 removed the remaining hereditary peers through ordinary legislation.

strands.title: Keeps decisions with elected MPs, not judges
strands.hint: Codification would give judges power to strike down laws.

questions.judgement: Codification would move power from Parliament to judges. Decide whether that is a gain in rights or a loss in accountability.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that devolution has strengthened the United Kingdom.

strands.title: Governments that reflect distinct electorates
strands.hint: Plaid Cymru's Rhun ap Iorwerth became the first non-Labour First Minister of Wales in May 2026.

strands.title: More power closer to people in England
strands.hint: The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 created a framework of 'strategic authorities', some led by elected mayors.

strands.title: Tension and independence pressure
strands.hint: Look for rows over funding, Sewel and independence.

strands.title: Unequal devolution
strands.hint: Four new mayoral elections were postponed to 2028 (announced Dec 2025).

questions.judgement: Devolution may strengthen the Union by accommodating nationalism, or weaken it by fuelling it.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that Parliament is an effective check on the executive.

strands.title: Backbench rebellions force U-turns
strands.hint: In July 2025, 49 Labour MPs voted against the welfare bill even after the PIP cuts were dropped.

strands.title: Select committees and humble addresses
strands.hint: In Feb 2026 MPs used a humble address to force the release of Peter Mandelson's vetting files.

strands.title: The Lords revise bills
strands.hint: Peers won changes to the Employment Rights Act 2025, including a six-month qualifying period for unfair-dismissal protection.

strands.title: Big majorities and the whips
strands.hint: The Immigration and Asylum Bill passed second reading 264–90 in July 2026.

strands.title: The executive controls the agenda
strands.hint: Governments set the legislative programme and use secondary legislation.

questions.judgement: Effectiveness depends on the government's majority and unity. 2025–26 shows backbenchers can bite.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the House of Lords is an effective chamber.

strands.title: Expertise and detailed revision
strands.hint: Crossbench experts scrutinise the detail of bills.

strands.title: Forces government concessions
strands.hint: The Lords forced concessions on the Employment Rights Bill (late 2025) and the Hereditary Peers Bill (Mar 2026).

strands.title: Lacks democratic legitimacy
strands.hint: Even after the last hereditary peers left (Apr 2026), every member is unelected.

strands.title: Limited powers
strands.hint: The Salisbury convention and the Parliament Acts limit the Lords' ability to block legislation.

questions.judgement: Effective at revising, weak at checking. Legitimacy remains the core problem.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that backbench MPs have significant influence over government.

strands.title: Rebellions and pressure on leaders
strands.hint: Ministerial resignations and MPs' loss of confidence were followed by Keir Starmer announcing his resignation (June 2026).

strands.title: Private members' bills and free votes
strands.hint: A revived assisted dying bill was defeated at second reading 270–286 (Sept 2026) on a free vote.

strands.title: Select committees
strands.hint: Committee chairs are elected by MPs and question ministers in public.

strands.title: Payroll vote and party discipline
strands.hint: Ministers and aides must vote with the government; rebels can lose the whip.

strands.title: Government controls time and legislation
strands.hint: Most parliamentary time goes on government business.

questions.judgement: Individually weak, collectively powerful, especially when a government's popularity falls.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the Prime Minister is dominant over the cabinet.

strands.title: Patronage and No 10 control
strands.hint: Andy Burnham removed 15 cabinet ministers when he formed his government (July 2026).

strands.title: PMs depend on cabinet and party support
strands.hint: Wes Streeting quit the cabinet saying he had lost confidence in Starmer (May 2026); Starmer announced his resignation in June.

strands.title: Events and external pressures
strands.hint: By-election defeats, poll slumps and market reactions all limit PMs.

questions.judgement: PM power is contingent on the majority, popularity, party unity and events.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that individual ministerial responsibility is still an important convention.

strands.title: Ministers still resign over conduct
strands.hint: Angela Rayner resigned in Sept 2025 after breaching the ministerial code over stamp duty.

strands.title: Officials take the blame
strands.hint: Olly Robbins, the Foreign Office's top civil servant, was sacked during the Mandelson vetting row (2026).

strands.title: Ministers survive if the PM backs them
strands.hint: Look for ministers who refuse to resign despite criticism.

questions.judgement: Resignations now depend more on political survival than on accepting responsibility.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that collective ministerial responsibility is still observed in UK government.

strands.title: Ministers resign when they can't support policy
strands.hint: Anneliese Dodds resigned over aid cuts (Feb 2025); John Healey and Al Carns resigned over defence spending (June 2026).

strands.title: Free votes and open splits
strands.hint: Assisted dying was a free vote: Labour MPs split 190 for, 153 against (Sept 2026).

questions.judgement: The convention bends to political need: suspended when useful, enforced when convenient.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the UK Supreme Court has significant influence over government.

strands.title: Landmark rulings shape policy
strands.hint: For Women Scotland (Apr 2025) ruled that 'woman' in the Equality Act means biological sex. The EHRC's revised code of practice followed in May 2026.

strands.title: Judicial review of ministers
strands.hint: Courts can rule that ministers acted unlawfully.

strands.title: Parliament can legislate around rulings
strands.hint: Parliamentary sovereignty means Parliament has the final word.

strands.title: Courts often defer to government
strands.hint: The Court of Appeal overturned the High Court and ruled the Palestine Action ban lawful in June 2026.

questions.judgement: Influence without supremacy: the court shapes policy through interpretation, but Parliament has the last word.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that Brexit restored parliamentary sovereignty.

strands.title: EU law no longer overrides Acts of Parliament
strands.hint: Parliament can now legislate without EU supremacy.

strands.title: The UK–EU reset brings back rule-taking
strands.hint: The European Partnership Bill (King's Speech, May 2026) allows dynamic alignment with EU rules for the SPS agrifood deal.

strands.title: Other constraints: ECHR, devolution, the people
strands.hint: Sovereignty is also limited by treaties, devolved institutions and referendums.

questions.judgement: Legal sovereignty was restored; political and practical sovereignty remain shared.

questions.text: To what extent do conservatives agree about the role of the state?

strands.title: Shared belief in order, authority and tradition
strands.hint: Link to Hobbes and Burke.

strands.title: One-nation paternalism vs New Right small state
strands.hint: Compare one-nation spending on public services with New Right tax cuts and deregulation (Oakeshott/Burke vs Rand/Nozick).

questions.judgement: Thinkers carry the marks: Hobbes, Burke, Oakeshott vs Rand and Nozick.

questions.text: To what extent do socialists agree on the role of the state in the economy?

strands.title: Common ownership and state control
strands.hint: Nationalisation (e.g. rail, steel) echoes traditional socialism (Marx, Luxemburg, Webb).

strands.title: Social democracy and the Third Way accept markets
strands.hint: Crosland backed 'state-managed capitalism': a mixed economy with full employment and welfare. Giddens's Third Way went further, accepting the free market and rejecting heavy state intervention.

questions.judgement: Marx and Luxemburg vs Crosland and Giddens: disagreement on means, agreement on equality as the goal.

questions.text: To what extent do liberals agree about the role of the state?

strands.title: Classical: freedom from interference
strands.hint: Locke and Mill: a limited state that protects liberty.

strands.title: Modern: an enabling state
strands.hint: Rawls and Friedan: welfare and equality of opportunity.

questions.judgement: Both strands share individualism; they disagree on whether the state threatens or enables freedom.

questions.text: To what extent is nationalism an inclusive ideology?

strands.title: Liberal and civic nationalism: self-determination for all
strands.hint: Link to Mazzini and Rousseau.

strands.title: Exclusive and expansionist nationalism
strands.hint: Link to Maurras. Expansionist claims on territory are current examples.

questions.judgement: Mazzini and Rousseau vs Maurras; Garvey on anti-colonial nationalism.

questions.text: To what extent do feminists agree on the nature of sex and gender?

strands.title: Shared goal of ending patriarchy and discrimination
strands.hint: Pay gaps and violence against women are common concerns.

strands.title: Divisions over sex and gender
strands.hint: The debate after For Women Scotland (Apr 2025) shows splits between gender-critical and trans-inclusive positions.

questions.judgement: de Beauvoir and Millett vs hooks and post-modern feminism.

questions.text: To what extent do ecologists agree on how to achieve sustainability?

strands.title: Shallow green: green growth within capitalism
strands.hint: Renewables and net zero targets without changing the economic system.

strands.title: Deep ecology and social ecology: systemic change
strands.hint: Leopold's land ethic, Bookchin (the crisis comes from social hierarchy) and Merchant (the domination of nature is linked to the domination of women). Schumacher's 'Buddhist economics' also rejects growth for its own sake.

questions.judgement: Shallow greens seek green growth within capitalism. Leopold, Schumacher, Bookchin and Merchant all demand deeper change but disagree about the cause: human attitudes, consumerism, social hierarchy or patriarchy.

questions.text: To what extent do multiculturalists agree about how diversity should be accommodated?

strands.title: Liberal multiculturalism: diversity within shared values
strands.hint: Link to Kymlicka.

strands.title: Pluralist multiculturalism
strands.hint: Parekh (rejects universalist liberalism; individuals are culturally embedded) and Modood (strong cultural identities alongside a shared national story).

questions.judgement: Kymlicka vs Parekh vs Modood.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the modern US presidency is an imperial presidency.

strands.title: Governing by executive action
strands.hint: Trump signed 225 executive orders in 2025 (Federal Register).

strands.title: Military action without Congress
strands.hint: US forces seized Venezuela's Maduro in January 2026 with no prior authorisation from Congress. The US–Israeli war on Iran from February 2026 prompted repeated war-powers votes.

strands.title: Control of the executive branch
strands.hint: Trump v. Slaughter (June 2026) overruled Humphrey's Executor, letting presidents remove FTC commissioners at will.

strands.title: The courts push back
strands.hint: Learning Resources v. Trump (Feb 2026, 6–3) struck down IEEPA tariffs. Trump v. Barbara (June 2026) struck down the birthright-citizenship order.

strands.title: Congress and public opinion constrain
strands.hint: Both chambers passed a non-binding Iran war-powers resolution in June 2026 (House 215–208, Senate 50–48). Trump's approval was about 35% in Sept 2026.

questions.judgement: 'Imperial' vs 'imperilled': power expands in foreign and emergency policy, but courts, Congress and elections still bite.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that Congress is an effective check on the president.

strands.title: Power of the purse
strands.hint: The 43-day shutdown (Oct–Nov 2025) and the 76-day DHS funding lapse (Feb–Apr 2026).

strands.title: Oversight and discharge petitions
strands.hint: A discharge petition forced a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which passed the House 427–1 (Nov 2025).

strands.title: Party loyalty in a narrow majority
strands.hint: A Venezuela war-powers resolution was killed 50–50, with VP Vance breaking the tie (Jan 2026).

strands.title: Gridlock and the filibuster
strands.hint: The filibuster lets a Senate minority block legislation.

questions.judgement: Congress checks most when the president's party is split or unpopular. Watch the 3 November 2026 midterms.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the US Supreme Court is more political than judicial.

strands.title: Ideological voting blocs
strands.hint: 22.7% of October Term 2025 decisions were ideological 6–3 splits (SCOTUSblog).

strands.title: The emergency docket shapes policy
strands.hint: The administration won 23 of 31 emergency applications decided by mid-Sept 2026 (Brennan Center).

strands.title: It rules against the president
strands.hint: The tariffs case (Learning Resources) and Trump v. Barbara both went against the administration.

strands.title: Legal reasoning and unanimity
strands.hint: 44% of October Term 2025 decisions were unanimous.

questions.judgement: Judicial philosophy (originalism vs living constitution) explains more than party loyalty.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that civil rights are effectively protected in the US today.

strands.title: Courts uphold core rights
strands.hint: Trump v. Barbara (June 2026) upheld birthright citizenship under the 14th Amendment.

strands.title: Voting rights weakened
strands.hint: Louisiana v. Callais (Apr 2026) sharply narrowed Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act.

strands.title: Immigration enforcement and civil liberties
strands.hint: Renée Good and Alex Pretti were killed by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January 2026.

strands.title: LGBTQ+ and DEI rollbacks
strands.hint: US v. Skrmetti (2025) and West Virginia v. B.P.J. (2026) upheld state restrictions affecting transgender people.

questions.judgement: Protection depends on which rights, which states and which branch. The Court is no longer the reliable guarantor it was in the Warren era.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that federalism is in decline in the US.

strands.title: Federal pressure on states
strands.hint: National Guard deployments to Los Angeles, DC and other cities (2025), and threats to cut funding to sanctuary jurisdictions.

strands.title: States resist and go their own way
strands.hint: California voters passed Prop 50 (64.4%, Nov 2025) to redraw House maps. Minnesota sued over Operation Metro Surge.

strands.title: Courts protect state power
strands.hint: Trump v. Illinois (Dec 2025) refused to allow the Chicago National Guard deployment.

questions.judgement: Federalism is contested, not dead: coercive federal action provokes energetic state resistance.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that money is the most important factor in US elections.

strands.title: Super PACs and mega-donors
strands.hint: The crypto super PAC Fairshake and its affiliates had more than $193m in cash on hand for the 2026 midterms by January 2026. NRSC v. FEC (June 2026) struck down limits on party coordinated spending.

strands.title: Money doesn't guarantee victory
strands.hint: Abdul El-Sayed beat AIPAC-backed Haley Stevens in Michigan's Senate primary (Aug 2026) despite heavy outside spending.

strands.title: Partisanship and the national mood
strands.hint: Democrats led the generic ballot by about 7.5 points in Sept 2026, with Trump's approval around 35%.

questions.judgement: Money is necessary but not sufficient. It matters most in primaries and open seats.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that congressional elections are no longer genuinely competitive.

strands.title: The redistricting war
strands.hint: Texas, California, Florida and other states redrew their House maps mid-decade in 2025–26.

strands.title: Incumbency advantage
strands.hint: Well over 90% of House incumbents who ran again in 2024 won.

strands.title: Primaries unseat incumbents
strands.hint: Sen. John Cornyn lost his Texas primary runoff to Ken Paxton (May 2026). Eleven House incumbents lost primaries in 2026.

strands.title: Open seats and toss-ups
strands.hint: There were 73 open House seats (Cook, Aug 2026), and Cook rated seven Senate races as toss-ups (Sept 2026).

questions.judgement: Competition has moved from general elections into primaries in most districts.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the Democratic and Republican parties are more divided internally than ever.

strands.title: Republican splits
strands.hint: Marjorie Taylor Greene resigned after a feud with Trump (effective Jan 2026). Rep. Kevin Kiley left the GOP (Mar 2026).

strands.title: Democratic splits
strands.hint: Insurgent wins for Zohran Mamdani (NYC, 2025) and Graham Platner (Maine, 2026), and pressure on Chuck Schumer.

strands.title: High party unity in Congress
strands.hint: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed the House 218–214 (July 2025), almost entirely on party lines.

questions.judgement: Parties are internally divided but externally polarised: they fight each other more than themselves.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that interest groups have too much influence in US politics.

strands.title: Money and access
strands.hint: Abdul El-Sayed overcame more than $60m in campaign spending, mostly from pro-Israel groups, to win Michigan's Senate primary (Aug 2026). The AI super PAC Leading the Future has raised over $140m.

strands.title: Pluralism, including rights groups
strands.hint: The ACLU and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund litigated key 2026 cases.

strands.title: Spending doesn't guarantee results
strands.hint: AIPAC-backed Haley Stevens lost the Michigan Senate primary (Aug 2026).

questions.judgement: Elitist vs pluralist theory: influence is real, but it is contested.

questions.text: Examine the differences between the US and UK Supreme Courts in their ability to check the executive.

strands.title: Can strike down executive actions under a sovereign constitution
strands.hint: E.g. Learning Resources v. Trump (2026) struck down IEEPA tariffs.

strands.title: Limited by parliamentary sovereignty
strands.hint: UK courts can rule that ministers acted unlawfully (judicial review) but cannot strike down Acts of Parliament.

questions.judgement: Examine questions need clear point-by-point comparison, not a verdict.

questions.text: Examine the differences between the US Congress and the UK Parliament in their ability to scrutinise the executive.

strands.title: Separation of powers: purse, oversight, confirmations
strands.hint: Shutdowns, subpoenas and Senate confirmations.

strands.title: Fusion of powers: PMQs, select committees, whips
strands.hint: Scrutiny from inside a government-dominated chamber.

questions.judgement: Structural differences (separation vs fusion of powers) explain most of the contrast.

questions.text: Analyse the differences between the party systems of the USA and the UK. In your answer you must consider the relevance of at least one comparative theory.

strands.title: Two-party dominance, weaker party discipline, primaries
strands.hint: Structural: primaries and federalism decentralise the parties.

strands.title: Multi-party votes, strong whips
strands.hint: Structural: FPTP and the fusion of powers. Cultural: class dealignment.

questions.judgement: Name the theory (rational, cultural or structural) and explain why it accounts for the difference.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the UN Security Council is ineffective in maintaining global peace and security.

strands.title: Vetoes paralyse it
strands.hint: China and Russia vetoed a Gulf-backed Hormuz shipping draft (Apr 2026). The US vetoed Gaza ceasefire drafts in 2025.

strands.title: Great powers act without it
strands.hint: The US seized Maduro in Caracas (Jan 2026) without UN authorisation; China called it illegal.

strands.title: Resolutions still authorise action
strands.hint: Resolution 2803 (Nov 2025, 13–0–2) endorsed the US plan for Gaza, welcomed the Board of Peace and authorised a temporary International Stabilization Force.

strands.title: Reform and renewal
strands.hint: UN80 reforms and the 2026 Secretary-General selection, with Security Council straw polls from July 2026.

questions.judgement: Effective where the P5's interests align (e.g. Haiti, the Gaza framework), paralysed where they clash (Ukraine, Iran).

questions.text: Evaluate the view that NATO remains an effective and relevant organisation.

strands.title: Deterrence and collective defence
strands.hint: Allies pledged 5% of GDP on defence by 2035 (The Hague, June 2025). Poland and Estonia invoked Article 4 in Sept 2025.

strands.title: Transatlantic tensions
strands.hint: In January 2026 Trump threatened tariffs on European allies over Greenland before backing down.

strands.title: Europe builds alternatives
strands.hint: The EU's €150bn SAFE defence loans and the Ukraine 'coalition of the willing'.

questions.judgement: NATO's relevance has grown with the Russian threat even as US commitment has become less predictable.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that global economic governance has failed to address global issues.

strands.title: Trade wars sideline the WTO
strands.hint: After the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs (Feb 2026), the US switched to Section 122 and then Section 301 tariffs.

strands.title: Poverty and debt persist
strands.hint: Look for debt distress, aid cuts and off-track development goals.

strands.title: IMF and World Bank crisis support
strands.hint: Emergency lending and debt relief.

strands.title: G7 and G20 coordination
strands.hint: The G7 (Évian, June 2026) launched a Critical Minerals Resilience and Production Alliance.

questions.judgement: Institutions reflect the power of their biggest members; they fail when the biggest member opts out.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that international courts have been ineffective in protecting human rights.

strands.title: Powerful states defy them
strands.hint: The US sanctioned ICC President Tomoko Akane (Aug 2026). The ICC warrants for Putin and Netanyahu remain unenforced.

strands.title: Slow and selective
strands.hint: South Africa v Israel at the ICJ is unlikely to be decided for years (written stages run to 2029).

strands.title: Accountability does happen
strands.hint: Charges against Rodrigo Duterte were confirmed (Apr 2026); his ICC trial opens on 30 November 2026.

strands.title: They set norms states must answer to
strands.hint: ICJ advisory opinions shape international law.

questions.judgement: Courts shape norms and occasionally deliver justice, but enforcement depends on states cooperating.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that humanitarian intervention is rarely successful.

strands.title: The world fails to act in the worst crises
strands.hint: The RSF took El Fasher, Sudan, in Oct 2025 after a siege of more than 500 days.

strands.title: Interventions look self-interested
strands.hint: The US presented its Venezuela operation (Jan 2026) as law enforcement rather than humanitarian action, and Trump spoke of bringing in US oil companies. This fits the realist critique that interventions serve self-interest.

strands.title: Authorised missions can help
strands.hint: UNSC Resolution 2793 turned the Haiti mission into a 5,500-strong Gang Suppression Force.

questions.judgement: Success depends on legitimacy (a UN mandate), clear aims and staying power.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that global environmental governance has been ineffective in tackling climate change.

strands.title: Major emitters walk away
strands.hint: The US left the Paris Agreement (effective 27 Jan 2026) and is leaving the UNFCCC (effective Feb 2027).

strands.title: Pledges fall short
strands.hint: UNEP's 2025 Emissions Gap Report projected 2.3–2.5°C of warming even if pledges are met.

strands.title: Agreements keep moving forward
strands.hint: COP30 (Belém, Nov 2025) agreed to triple adaptation finance by 2035. COP31 meets in Antalya, 9–20 Nov 2026.

strands.title: Law and litigation raise pressure
strands.hint: The ICJ gave an advisory opinion on states' climate obligations in July 2025.

questions.judgement: Consensus-based, mostly non-binding governance struggles with the 'tragedy of the commons'.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the world is now multipolar.

strands.title: Rising powers and the Global South
strands.hint: BRICS (11 members plus 10 partners) met in New Delhi in Sept 2026. Pakistan, Qatar, Egypt and Turkey all mediated conflicts in 2026.

strands.title: US hard power is unmatched
strands.hint: US military action in Venezuela and Iran (2026).

strands.title: A US–China bipolar rivalry
strands.hint: The Busan trade truce (Oct 2025) and Xi Jinping's state visit to Washington (Sept 2026).

questions.judgement: Economic multipolarity and military unipolarity, with a US–China rivalry at the core.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the EU is a significant global actor.

strands.title: Economic and sanctions power
strands.hint: EU sanctions packages on Russia (20th in Apr 2026, 21st in July 2026) and a €90bn loan to Ukraine for 2026–27.

strands.title: Enlargement and normative power
strands.hint: Accession negotiating clusters opened for Ukraine and Moldova in June–July 2026.

strands.title: Divisions and reliance on the US
strands.hint: Unanimity rules let single states block action.

strands.title: Concessions in trade with the US
strands.hint: The July 2025 EU–US 'Turnberry' deal capped US tariffs on most EU goods at 15%.

questions.judgement: An economic and regulatory superpower, but a military and diplomatic middleweight.

questions.text: Evaluate the view that globalisation has undermined state sovereignty.

strands.title: Global shocks no state can control
strands.hint: Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz (Mar 2026) sent Brent crude to about $126.

strands.title: States are reasserting control
strands.hint: The US announced its withdrawal from 66 international bodies (Jan 2026). Trump told the UN 'there is no global government' (Sept 2026).

questions.judgement: Globalisation constrains weak states far more than powerful ones.

questions.text: Analyse the divisions between realists and liberals over the role of international organisations. In your answer you must discuss any relevant core political ideas.

strands.title: States act in self-interest; organisations reflect power
strands.hint: Vetoes and unilateral action.

strands.title: Institutions enable cooperation
strands.hint: Resolutions, agreements and interdependence.

questions.judgement: Link realism to conservative ideas about human nature, and liberalism to liberal ideas about rationality and progress.

questions.text: Examine the differences between the EU and one other regional organisation in how far they address contemporary global issues.

strands.title: Supranational institutions, sanctions and a single market
strands.hint: The Commission, sanctions packages and trade deals.

strands.title: Intergovernmental and consensus-based
strands.hint: E.g. ASEAN, the African Union, USMCA.

questions.judgement: Compare depth of integration, decision-making and capacity to act.
